title: Standard Normal
text: How quickly does Normal happen when the parent population is already Standard Normal? It happens immediately. A linear combination of independent Normal variables is Normal, so the sample mean is exactly Normal at every positive sample size. The smallest defensible answer is therefore \(n=1\).

title: Standard Normal

A linear combination of independent Normal variables is Normal, so the sample mean is exactly Normal at every positive sample size. The smallest defensible answer is therefore \(n=1\).

2. Parent population

title: Standard Normal
text:
3. Theory before simulation
For independent \(X_i \sim N(0,1)\),
\[
\bar X_n \sim N\left(0,\frac{1}{n}\right).
\]
The center is 0 and the standard error is \(1/\sqrt{n}\). No approximation is involved.

title: Standard Normal
text:
4. Simulation design
At every evaluated \(n\), I generated 10,000 independent sample means with seed 631. The simulated diagnostics calibrate the amount of random fluctuation expected even when Normality is exact.

title: Standard Normal
text:
9. Decision and diagnostic agreement
Decision: \(n=1\). Theory is decisive, and the numerical and graphical evidence agree. The calibration results show why a finite simulation should never be expected to produce exactly zero skewness, exactly zero excess kurtosis, or a perfect Q-Q line.

title: Standard Normal
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
The apparent roughness of a histogram depends on binning, and the largest simulated calibration fluctuation depends on the chosen grid. The important surprise is conceptual: increasing \(n\) improves precision here, but it does not make the standardized shape more Normal. It was already Normal.

title: Six-Sided Die

Figure 1: Each die face has probability 1/6. The parent is perfectly symmetric but discrete, which separates the effects of asymmetry and lattice spacing.

title: Six-Sided Die
text:
3. Theory before simulation
For one fair die, \(E(X)=3.5\) and \(Var(X)=35/12\). Independence, identical distribution, and finite variance hold, so
\[
E(\bar X_n)=3.5, \qquad SE(\bar X_n)=\sqrt{\frac{35}{12n}}.
\]
The ordinary CLT applies.

title: Six-Sided Die
text:
9. Decision and disagreement
Decision: \(n=30\). The histogram is symmetric and sufficiently smooth for a practical Normal approximation, the center and SE are accurate, and the conclusion remains credible at \(n=40\) and \(n=50\). Q-Q RMSE still exceeds the stringent Normal-noise band. I retain that disagreement because it correctly detects lattice spacing, but it does not make the global approximation misleading.

title: Six-Sided Die
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
The selected threshold depends on the intended use. A continuity-sensitive tail calculation may need a larger \(n\) than a central probability approximation. The notable surprise is that symmetry solves the skewness problem immediately, while discreteness leaves a longer numerical fingerprint.

title: Small Binomial
text:
3. Theory before simulation
The parent mean is \(5(0.10)=0.5\) and variance is \(5(0.10)(0.90)=0.45\). Independent identical observations are bounded, so the ordinary CLT applies and
\[
SE(\bar X_n)=\sqrt{\frac{0.45}{n}}.
\]
Discreteness does not violate the theorem, but it can remain visible in finite samples.

title: Small Binomial
text:

The grid is dense from \(n=1\) to 200, then checks 300 and 500 for stability. Every grid point uses 10,000 means and seed 631. Because the transition is borderline, \(n=200\), 300, and 500 are repeated with seed 1631.

9. Decision and disagreement
Decision: \(n=200\). The center, SE, global histogram, and skewness support a practical Normal approximation, and the judgment persists at \(n=300\) and \(n=500\) under both seeds. title: Small Binomial

10. Limitation and surprise
The threshold is specific to size 5 and probability 0.10. A rarer-success Binomial would converge more slowly. The surprise is that the discrete grid remains measurable after the histogram already looks convincingly bell-shaped.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Five parent populations enter. Their sample means do not all approach the bell curve at the same pace, and one never does.
This project uses repeated sampling to ask a practical version of the Central Limit Theorem: how large must the sample be before a Normal approximation is genuinely useful? Each analysis begins with a prediction, checks the theorem, and then compares graphical and numerical evidence.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Answer first
The parent distribution matters enormously. Standard Normal needs no waiting: \(n=1\) is exact. A symmetric die is useful by \(n=30\). The skewed small Binomial needs about \(n=200\), and Exponential needs about \(n=300\). Standard Cauchy never reaches an ordinary-CLT threshold because its sample mean remains Cauchy at every \(n\).


Show R code
thresholds <- data.frame(
  population = factor(c("Standard Normal", "Six-sided die", "Small Binomial", "Exponential"), levels = rev(c("Standard Normal", "Six-sided die", "Small Binomial", "Exponential"))),
  n = c(1, 30, 200, 300),
  color = c("#0d6973", "#3a7697", "#8b4f79", "#bd5b32")
)
ggplot(thresholds, aes(n, population)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 30, color = "#d8a23c", linetype = "22", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = n, yend = population, color = color), linewidth = 1.1, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_point(aes(color = color), size = 4.2, show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_text(aes(label = paste0("n = ", n)), nudge_y = 0.22, fontface = "bold", color = "#173f47") +
  scale_color_identity() +
  scale_x_log10(breaks = c(1, 10, 30, 100, 300), limits = c(1, 400)) +
  labs(x = "Smallest defensible sample size, log scale", y = NULL) +
  analysis_theme(base_size = 13)








Figure 1: Smallest defensible sample sizes for the four finite-variance cases. The n = 30 marker highlights the familiar rule of thumb: it works for the symmetric die, not for the two skewed parents. Cauchy is excluded because no ordinary-CLT threshold exists.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
The five investigations

Standard Normal: an exact reference case at every sample size.
Six-sided die: bounded, discrete, and symmetric.
Exponential: continuous with a long right tail.
Small Binomial: discrete, zero-heavy, and right-skewed.
Standard Cauchy: a stress test with no finite mean or variance.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
What each diagnostic contributed

Center: all finite-variance cases centered correctly well before their shapes were convincing.
Standard error: the theoretical \(\sigma/\sqrt{n}\) relationship worked early and did not by itself certify Normality.
Skewness: this separated the symmetric die from the two asymmetric parents.
Excess kurtosis: this exposed tail and peak differences that skewness could miss.
Q-Q RMSE: this was the strictest diagnostic, especially for discrete lattices.
Plots: these determined whether the remaining numerical departure would materially mislead a Normal approximation.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Evidence standard
The final decision does not come from a single score. Center, standard error, skewness, excess kurtosis, a Q-Q discrepancy, and the plots each answer a different question. Numerical bands are calibrated against the finite simulation noise in the Normal case. A conclusion must also persist for the next two larger evaluated sample sizes.






NoteWhy n = 30 is not a law



At \(n=30\), the die is defensible, Exponential still shows substantial right-tail curvature, and the small Binomial remains skewed and visibly discrete. Sample size cannot be judged apart from the parent shape and the intended use of the approximation.

title: How Fast Does Normal Happen?
text:
Reproducibility and limits
All final results use seed 631 and 10,000 repetitions per sample size. The borderline small-Binomial conclusion was repeated with seed 1631 and remained in the same transition region. The simulations cannot prove a universal threshold, and tail-sensitive applications may require larger samples than the practical whole-distribution judgments here.
See the methodology decisions and curated AI interaction log for the full decision trail.

title: Standard Cauchy
text: Can a huge sample rescue an average from a standard Cauchy parent? No. The population has no finite mean or variance, so the ordinary CLT does not apply. I predicted persistent heavy tails at every \(n\).

title: Standard Cauchy

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
2. Parent population


Show R code
plot_parent_population(population)








Figure 1: The central standard-Cauchy density resembles a bell, but its tails decay too slowly for a finite mean or variance. Central appearance alone is therefore deceptive.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
3. Theory before simulation
If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are independent standard Cauchy variables, then
\[
\frac{X_1+\cdots+X_n}{n} \sim Cauchy(0,1).
\]
The sample mean has exactly the same distribution for every \(n\). Population mean, variance, and theoretical SE are unavailable, so reporting them would be mathematically false.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
4. Simulation design
I simulated 10,000 means at each of \(n=1,2,5,10,30,100,500,\) and 1000 with seed 631. All observations, including extremes, enter the quantiles and maximum. Histograms show only the declared central window \([-10,10]\) and report the omitted fraction.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
7. Why ordinary diagnostics are absent
Sample SD, moment skewness, and moment kurtosis exist for a finite simulated batch, but they are dominated by whichever rare extreme appears. They do not estimate stable Cauchy population moments. I therefore mark center, theoretical SE, relative SE error, skewness, excess kurtosis, and Normal Q-Q RMSE unavailable rather than presenting unstable numbers as comparable evidence.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
8. Robust comparison
For a standard Cauchy, the theoretical 1st and 99th percentiles are approximately -31.82 and 31.82, and the IQR is exactly 2. The simulated values in the table remain close across \(n\), even while the maximum varies wildly. Robust center and spread tell the stable story better than sample variance.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
9. Decision
Decision: no ordinary-CLT threshold exists. The failure is theoretical and empirical. Larger samples do not narrow the distribution of the mean, and persistent extreme means are part of the result rather than data errors.

title: Standard Cauchy
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
Any finite simulation understates some possible tail events, and a central plot cannot display an unbounded range. The striking surprise is that averaging 1,000 observations changes neither the law nor the typical IQR of the mean. More data do not repair a missing first moment.

title: Exponential
text: The Exponential parent is continuous but strongly right-skewed. I expected the ordinary CLT to work, yet much more slowly than for the symmetric die because averaging must tame a long right tail.

title: Exponential
text:
3. Theory before simulation
For \(X_i \sim Exp(1)\), \(E(X)=1\) and \(Var(X)=1\). All ordinary CLT conditions hold, giving center 1 and theoretical standard error \(1/\sqrt{n}\).
The exact sample sum is Gamma, so the remaining standardized skewness shrinks like \(2/\sqrt{n}\). This predicts slow but steady progress.

title: Exponential
text:
9. Decision and disagreement
Decision: \(n=300\). Center and SE have long since stabilized, skewness reaches the practical 0.10 band, and the remaining tail curvature is not large enough to misrepresent the main distribution. The judgment persists at \(n=500\) and \(n=750\). Q-Q RMSE remains stricter than the visual decision, which warns that sensitive extreme-tail work may still need more data.

title: Exponential
text:
10. Limitation and surprise
A single threshold cannot serve every tail probability. The most useful surprise is how early the mean and SE look correct compared with the shape: first and second moments alone would have declared victory much too soon.
